1.goal: To open the lesson on a piece of news she chose, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
run: Ask whether she did the pre-class and whether anything in it was unclear.
Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she reads an article full of numbers and briefs a director who has not read it.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “Today you read a news article with a lot of numbers. Then you brief a director who has not read it.”
If she answers in general terms: “Which company were you thinking of, and what could change for the people there?”
1.expected: One piece of news from this week and the company it made her think of, in two or three sentences. A complete answer looks like “The price of oil went up again, and I thought about my old company, because transport costs would go up.” — the news, the company, and the link between them. Any news she brings is right here.
1.support: If nothing comes to mind, name two areas and let her pick one: something in the economy, or something in the world that affects transport or energy.
1.challenge: Ask which number in that story she would want to check before repeating it.
1.monitoring: Whether a number appears in her answer, and how she says it.
1.evidence: The news she brought, in her words.
1.transition: Move on when she has named one piece of news and a company.

2.goal: To establish who is asking, what the director needs, and what she should leave the conversation with.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the brief with her.
Ask the question on screen and let her answer in one sentence.
2.expected: Something close to “The director needs to know what the numbers say and which ones are measured and which are an estimate.” Both parts are in the last two lines of the brief; the figures themselves are not named here.
2.support: If she answers with what the article might say, point at “What you want by the end” and read it with her.
2.challenge: Ask what she would want to know about the director before briefing them.
2.monitoring: Whether she states the task from the brief or starts guessing the content.
2.evidence: Whether she can say the task in one sentence without rereading.
2.transition: Move on when she has said, in one sentence, what the director needs.

3.goal: To have her commit to three guesses before she reads, so the reading has something to confirm.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. Nothing is confirmed or corrected here.
run: Read the three questions with her.
Take one answer on each and leave them unconfirmed: the article on the next screen settles them.
Note her three answers where she can see them.
exact: Before moving on: “Those are your guesses. Now we read and see.”
3.expected: There is no answer key on this screen: the three questions are open. For your reference, the article will show overtime going up and ships arriving in groups, turnover rising at the largest site, and figures from three sources — the company, the carriers and a consultancy.
3.support: If she answers about logistics in general, ask her to answer as if it were a distribution center she knows.
3.challenge: Ask which of her three guesses she would bet on, and why.
3.monitoring: Whether she draws on her own experience in logistics HR.
3.evidence: Her three guesses, kept for screen 4.
3.transition: Move on when all three questions have an answer, right or wrong.

4.goal: To read the article once for the story: what happened, and what the company has not published or decided.
run: Give her about three minutes for the article.
Ask the question on screen.
Then ask which of her guesses from screen 3 the article confirms.
4.expected: What happened: a shipping route closed and ships take a longer way around; at Norvale Logistics overtime went up and voluntary turnover at the largest site rose. What the company has not done: it “has not published what the departures cost” and “has not decided whether to hire temporary staff.”
4.support: If she lists numbers, ask her to say the story first without any number.
4.challenge: Ask which part of the article a finance director would read first.
4.monitoring: Whether she reads for the whole or stops on the figures.
4.evidence: How long she takes, and whether she reads the article once or goes back while answering.
4.transition: Move on when she has said what happened and the two things the company has not done.

5.goal: To attribute each of six statements to the source in the article that gives it, going back to the line instead of answering from memory.
5.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S to check.
run: Let her place all six on her own and press Check when she has finished. The button checks the whole activity at once.
Then go through the six out loud. On each, ask her to open the article with the button on screen and read the line that decides it.
Spend the time that is left on the total cost.
exact: On each statement: “Which line says that? Read it to me.”
On the total cost: “The article has the number $233,800. Is it Norvale saying what the departures cost?”
5.expected: The company: “Overtime hours rose 18.4% between April and June.” (“…, the company says.”) · “Turnover at the largest site reached 14.6% in the second quarter.” (“Company figures show…”). The carriers: “The detour adds nine to twelve days to each trip.” · “The route will reopen by the end of the year.” (“The carriers expect…”). The consultancy: “Replacing one warehouse worker costs about $4,870.” Nobody in the article: “The departures cost Norvale $233,800.” — Norvale “has not published what the departures cost”; the figure is the consultancy estimate multiplied by 48, and the article says the 48 people “would represent roughly” that amount.
5.support: If she answers from memory, open the article and ask her to find the line before she chooses.
5.challenge: Ask which of the six a finance director would most likely repeat wrongly in a meeting.
5.monitoring: Whether she goes back to the article. The total cost is where attribution and status meet; if she places it with the consultancy, it is close — ask what the consultancy actually estimated.
5.evidence: Whether she returned to the article, and what she did with the total cost.
5.transition: Move on when the six are placed and the total cost has been discussed.

6.goal: To have her notice that small words around a figure tell the reader who gives it, whether it is exact, and whether it has happened.
6.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S.
run: Let her classify the six words and phrases and press Check.
Go through them out loud. On each, ask her to find it in the article and read the whole sentence.
Then ask her what happens to each sentence if the word is taken out.
exact: After the check: “Take out ‘roughly’ and ‘would represent’. What does the director hear now?”
6.expected: Who the information comes from: “the company says” · “according to two of the largest carriers”. The figure is not exact: “roughly” · “would represent”. It has not happened yet: “expect the route to reopen” · “has not decided whether”. Without “roughly” and “would represent”, the sentence says the 48 people cost $233,800 — a fact nobody in the article gives.
6.support: On each phrase, ask: does it tell you who, how exact, or when?
6.challenge: Ask for one more word in the article that marks an estimate. “About” before $4,870 is one; “estimates” is another.
6.monitoring: Whether she sees the job of each word in context. She reads fast and may classify by the word alone.
6.evidence: Which of the two “not exact” phrases she placed elsewhere, if any.
6.transition: Move on when the six are sorted and she has said what changes without the words.

7.goal: To have her find that “5.4 percent” and “5.4 percentage points” describe different changes, and to hear the forms that say the article’s change correctly.
run: Read the question and the three sentences with her.
Let her answer before you open the button.
Open the difference and read it with her. Then ask her to describe the change in overtime or in turnover in one sentence of her own.
exact: If she does not see it: “If turnover rose 5.4 percent from 9.2, where does it end up?”
Asking for her own sentence: “Tell me how turnover changed, in a way the director cannot misread.”
7.expected: “Turnover rose 5.4 percent.” is the different one: it means turnover grew by 5.4% of 9.2, to about 9.7%. “Turnover rose from 9.2 to 14.6 percent.” and “Turnover rose 5.4 percentage points.” both say what the article says. From the reveal: the two figures (“from 9.2 to 14.6 percent”), the gap in percentage points (“5.4 percentage points”), or the change compared with where it started (“up by more than half”).
7.support: Write 9.2 and 14.6 where she can see them and ask her to subtract.
7.challenge: Ask what “turnover more than doubled” would mean with these figures, and whether it is true.
7.monitoring: Whether she finds the difference before the reveal, and whether her own sentence uses percentage points or the two figures.
7.evidence: Her own sentence about the change, word for word.
7.transition: Move on when the reveal has been read and she has said one sentence of her own.

8.goal: To say the figures of the article in full, with the source in the same sentence, before the briefing.
8.interaction: T–S, spoken, one figure at a time.
run: Play the five sentences once, and ask her to say each one after it.
Then ask for three figures a director would ask about first, one at a time, each with its source.
When a number is rounded or the source is missing, ask her to say the sentence again.
Open the model briefing after she has said her three figures, and ask where the sources and the estimates are in it.
exact: Asking for the first one: “The turnover. Tell me, and say where it comes from.”
Rebuilding a rounded number: “Say the exact figure. Four thousand…”
8.expected: Three sentences of this kind, each with its source and the number in full: “According to the company, overtime hours rose eighteen point four percent.”, “Company figures show turnover went from nine point two to fourteen point six percent.” and “A consultancy estimates about four thousand eight hundred seventy dollars to replace one worker.” Any form that keeps the source and the exact figure together is correct, including forms not on the screen.
8.support: If a number stalls, say its first half and let her finish it.
8.challenge: Ask for the total cost in one sentence that makes clear it is a calculation on an estimate.
8.monitoring: Which numbers she says in full and which she rounds; where the source lands.
8.evidence: The numbers she rounded or swapped, if any.
8.transition: Move on when three figures have been said with their sources.

9.goal: To brief the director she chose on the article, with each figure and its source, the estimates marked, and her own reading marked as hers, with the sentence starters closed.
9.interaction: Role-play. You are the director from the option she chose; she briefs you.
run: Read the two options and the list on screen with her, and let her choose.
Let her run until she has given at least two figures. Then interrupt once, with the question for her option, and let her go back to where she was.
The sentence starters stay closed. Open them only if she stops, let her look, and close them again.
Leave corrections for screen 11. Write down one sentence with a number, as she said it.
exact: Interruption, option A (HR director): “Sorry — is that 14.6 percent of everyone at the company, or only at one site?”
Interruption, option B (finance director): “Wait. Is the $233,800 their own number?”
9.expected: Five things in one turn, in the order of the list: what the article is about; the figures that matter to that director, each with its source (for A, the overtime and the turnover at the largest site; for B, the $4,870 estimate and the roughly $233,800); the estimates marked as estimates; an answer to the interruption (A: only at Norvale’s largest site; B: no — Norvale has not published a cost, it is the consultancy estimate multiplied by 48); and what she thinks the director should look at, marked as her reading.
9.support: If she stops, point at the next item on the list before you open the starters.
9.challenge: Ask which figure she would check before repeating it in a meeting, and why.
9.monitoring: Numbers in full, sources in the sentence, estimates marked — and what she does in the first seconds after the interruption.
9.evidence: One sentence of the briefing with a number, written word for word. It goes into the boards on screen 11.
9.transition: Move on when she has given the figures and said what the director should look at.

10.goal: To keep the conversation going after the briefing: answer two questions from the director, one of which the article does not answer, and ask one back.
10.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are still the director from her option.
run: Ask the two questions for her option, one at a time.
After each answer, wait. Give her time to add the source or to mark her reading.
Then ask her to put one question to you about your own sites, and answer it.
exact: Option A, question 1: “Are people really leaving because of the schedules, or is that just what they say in exit interviews?”
Option A, question 2: “If this happened at one of our sites, what number would you want to see first?”
Option B, question 1: “So how much are the departures actually costing them?”
Option B, question 2: “Would you hire temporary staff in their place?”
Handing the turn over: “Is there anything you want to ask me?”
10.expected: Two answers that say where they come from, and one question from her. Option A, question 1: the article only reports that exit interviews “point to” the schedules, said by the HR director — a complete answer marks the rest as her reading, for example “The article only has the exit interviews on that. My reading is that the schedules matter, but I would check the overtime by site.” Question 2 has no answer in the article, so any figure she names, marked as her recommendation, is correct. Option B, question 1: nobody knows — Norvale has not published it; on the consultancy estimate the 48 departures would represent roughly $233,800. Question 2 is not decided in the article; any answer marked as her recommendation is correct. Her question can be as small as “Do you want me to check our own turnover by site?”.
10.support: If she answers without a source, ask “Is that in the article?” and wait.
10.challenge: Push back once: “But $233,800 is a lot of money. Why can I not use it?” Let her answer from the line.
10.monitoring: Whether she marks her reading when the article has no answer, and whether she stays in English when the question is not the one she expected.
10.evidence: Whether she marked her reading without being asked, whether she asked a question of her own, and whether Portuguese appeared.
10.transition: Move on when she has answered the two questions and asked one.

11.goal: To give one piece of feedback she can use, and to run the briefing again for the director from the other option.
11.interaction: T–S, filling the boards together, then the replay.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve in the boards on screen.
Write the sentence you noted on screen 9 as she said it, and build a clearer version with her in the fourth box.
Open the replay. You now play the director from the option she did not choose. She briefs you, starting with what matters most to that director.
exact: Opening the replay, as the HR director: “I only care about the people. What is happening to them?”
Opening the replay, as the finance director: “Give me the money first. How sure is it?”
11.expected: The same article briefed to the other director, with a different figure first and the sources kept. A complete second version for the finance director sounds like “What matters most for you here is the cost. The company has not published one; a consultancy estimates about $4,870 per worker, so the 48 people who left would represent roughly $233,800.” For the HR director, it starts with the turnover at the largest site, from 9.2% to 14.6%.
11.support: Point at the line on screen and let her use it word for word the first time.
11.challenge: Interrupt once more, with a question she has not heard yet, and let her go back to where she was.
11.monitoring: Whether the point to improve from the boards appears in the replay.
11.evidence: Whether the point to improve changed in the second version.
11.transition: Move on when the replay has been said.

12.goal: To close on what was worked on, let her say how confident she feels, and leave the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “This week, when you pass on a number from the news, say where it comes from in the same sentence.”
12.expected: The recap has seven lines, and all seven were done if the lesson ran to the end: reading the article for the story, saying who gives each figure, telling a measured figure from an estimate and an expectation, comparing percentages in percentage points, saying broken numbers in full with the source, answering the interruption and going back, and answering the director’s questions. The confidence scale is hers, and it may come out lower than what you saw.
12.support: If she marks everything low, name one number she said in full today, with its source.
12.challenge: Ask where she will use percentage points this week.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed. The gap is worth noting.
12.evidence: Her confidence marks, and anything she said about the pre-class.
12.transition: End here. The next lesson is a call where a finance director interrupts a presentation with questions nobody prepared.
